questions.q: Why can't a pure chat model reliably answer a question like 'what's our current refund policy,' per this lesson's example?
options: Chat models are incapable of answering any factual question
The policy text may not already be in its context, so it can only guess or admit it doesn't know — it has no way to go check
Refund policy questions are always outside any model's training data
Only agents are allowed to discuss company policies
questions.explain: Without a tool call and a loop to use it, a chat-only model is stuck with whatever's already in its context — it can't go look something up and incorporate the result.

questions.q: What is the simple test this lesson proposes for whether a task needs a real agent loop?
options: Whether the task description is longer than one sentence
Whether the user is a paying customer
Whether it would be fun to build with an agent
Whether answering well requires information discovered through more than one step, where later steps depend on earlier results
questions.explain: If a task doesn't need multi-step, interdependent discovery, a single prompt (or at most a fixed workflow) is enough — no real agent loop is needed.

questions.q: Does the model itself ever execute a tool?
options: Yes, Claude runs the tool directly on Anthropic's servers for every tool
No — for tools you define, the model only requests a call via a tool_use block; your application code actually executes it
Only if the tool is written in Python
Yes, but only for tools named 'get_weather'
questions.explain: For your own tools, the model requests the call with a tool_use block; your code is responsible for actually running it and sending back a tool_result.

questions.q: If you want Claude to both call a specific tool AND provide natural-language commentary in the same turn, what does this lesson recommend?
options: This is impossible under any circumstances
Always use tool_choice: {"type": "none"} instead
Use tool_choice: {"type": "auto"} and explicitly ask for the tool in the prompt, rather than forcing with "any" or "tool"
Send the request twice with two different tool_choice values simultaneously
questions.explain: Forcing with any/tool suppresses commentary by design; using auto plus an explicit instruction in the prompt lets Claude both narrate and still call the intended tool.

questions.q: What does 'meaningful namespacing' in tool names (e.g., github_list_prs, slack_send_message) accomplish?
options: It makes tool selection unambiguous as the tool library spans multiple services and grows larger
It is required for a tool's input_schema to be valid JSON
It automatically reduces the number of tokens a tool definition uses
It has no practical effect on model behavior
questions.explain: Prefixing names by service keeps tools from one system from being confused with similarly-named tools from another as the overall set grows.

questions.q: What does Claude's response look like when it calls more than one tool in a single turn?
options: The API returns an error, since only one tool call is allowed per turn
A single tool_use block that lists multiple tool names inside it
A content array containing multiple separate tool_use blocks, each with its own id
Two completely separate API responses sent simultaneously
questions.explain: By default, Claude may call multiple tools in one response — the content array simply contains more than one tool_use block, each independently identified.

questions.q: What problem does 'reasoning only, no acting' run into, per this lesson?
options: It runs too fast and completes tasks too quickly
It uses no tokens at all
The model can reason fluently but has no way to check its reasoning against the real world, risking a confident, wrong answer
It is literally impossible for a language model to reason without acting
questions.explain: Without grounding reasoning in real tool results, a model's reasoning chain can drift into a plausible-sounding but incorrect conclusion.

questions.q: What determines which of the three memory mechanisms (conversation history, scratchpad, external memory) is the right choice for a given agent's accumulated state?
options: The programming language the agent happens to be written in
How long the state needs to persist and how much of it needs to stay immediately accessible versus retrieved on demand
Whether the agent has ever called a tool named 'get_weather'
The mechanism is always the same regardless of the situation
questions.explain: The three mechanisms trade off differently on persistence and accessibility — the right choice depends on the actual shape of the task's state needs, not a one-size-fits-all default.

questions.q: What real cost does planning add on top of what Lesson 5 already identified for agent loops in general?
options: No additional cost of any kind — planning is always free
Planning removes all token costs from every subsequent step
Planning makes every tool call guaranteed to succeed with zero errors
The latency of the planning step itself, on top of the per-iteration costs an agent loop already carries
questions.explain: Generating the plan upfront is itself an extra model call with its own latency, stacked on top of the loop costs (latency, tokens, failure surface) Lesson 5 already covered.

questions.q: What is meant by a "compounding error" in an agent's multi-step loop?
options: An error that only ever affects the final output, never intermediate steps
A mistake the agent doesn't catch, which it then treats as true and builds its next decision on top of
An error caused exclusively by a network timeout
A bug that only occurs when two agents run at the same time
questions.explain: Because an agent observes its own prior results to decide its next action, an uncaught mistake doesn't stay isolated — the agent treats it as ground truth and takes a further action on top of it, compounding the problem.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend persisting a pending approval request and stopping the loop, rather than blocking synchronously while waiting for a human?
options: Synchronous blocking is not supported by any programming language
A process that blocks waiting on a human response is fragile and expensive to keep running; a durable, resumable queue is what makes this workable in production
Persisting requests is required by the Claude API's terms of service
It has no practical benefit over synchronous blocking
questions.explain: Humans can take minutes or hours to respond; keeping a process alive and blocked the whole time doesn't scale. Persisting the pending request lets the loop resume later once a decision is made.

options: It immediately approves the action if no one responds within a second
It deletes the pending request after a fixed window
If the assigned approver hasn't responded within a set window, the request automatically routes to a different or broader set of reviewers
It disables the tool entirely after a timeout
questions.explain: Timeout escalation reassigns a stalled request to a second reviewer or a broader queue after a defined window, rather than leaving it indefinitely with one person.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say tool access specifically raises the stakes of an indirect prompt injection?
options: Tool access has no effect on the severity of prompt injection

A chatbot that reads poisoned content might just produce odd text, but an agent with tool access can be steered into actually taking a real action — sending data, modifying a record — based on injected instructions
Agents with tools are immune to prompt injection by design
Tool access only matters for direct prompt injection, not indirect
questions.explain: An agent is designed to act on what it reads, not just comment on it, so an injected instruction that reaches a tool-using agent can translate into a real, consequential action rather than just a strange sentence.

questions.q: What does environment isolation (e.g., a sandbox with an egress allowlist and a read-only filesystem) protect against that credential scoping alone does not?
options: It has no distinct purpose from credential scoping
It bounds where a tool's code actually executes — network, filesystem, and system access — so that even a tool working exactly as intended can't reach beyond its sandbox
It only matters for tools that never make any API calls
It replaces the need for cost budgets entirely
questions.explain: Credential scope limits what an agent can reach through APIs it calls; environment isolation limits what its executing code itself can touch (filesystem, network, other processes), covering a different surface.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a "max repeat calls" limit in addition to a max iteration count?
options: It catches a loop retrying the identical tool call with the same input expecting a different result — a common failure that should trigger a stop faster than a general iteration cap would
It replaces the need for a max iteration count entirely
It is only useful for tools that require human approval
It has no distinct purpose from the max wall-clock limit
questions.explain: Max repeat calls targets the narrow, very common case of literally retrying the same failing call — since that pattern is easy to detect, this limit should trip fastest, often after just two identical attempts.

questions.q: Why does this lesson use MAX_ITERATIONS = 8 and budget_usd = 0.50 instead of the larger numbers used as general examples in Lessons 23 and 24?
options: Because these are hard-coded values that must always be used for every agent

Because this specific refund-lookup task genuinely needs fewer iterations and less budget than an open-ended task, illustrating Lesson 24's point that budgets should be sized per task, not copy-pasted generically
Because the Claude API enforces these exact limits automatically
Because larger numbers are not technically supported by the API
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes these numbers are task-specific — a refund lookup is cheap and bounded, so its budget and iteration cap are set smaller than a general-purpose example would need.

questions.q: In the capstone's two tool schemas, why does issue_refund's description explicitly state that it requires human approval, if the description itself doesn't enforce that?
options: It has no real purpose and is purely decorative
It's good practice so the model's own explanations of its plan reflect reality, even though the actual enforcement happens in your application code, not the description text
The Claude API requires this exact phrase in every tool description
It replaces the need for any code-level checkpoint
questions.explain: The description helps the model's own behavior (how it explains what it's about to do) match reality, but the lesson is explicit that your code — not the description — is what actually enforces the checkpoint.

questions.q: What is the capstone project built across Lessons 29-31?
options: A five-tool multi-agent orchestration system
A support agent with two tools — a read-only get_order and a consequential issue_refund — that applies the safety patterns from Chapters 4 and 5
A chatbot with no tool access at all
A tool that only generates marketing copy
questions.explain: The capstone is deliberately scoped to one read-only tool and one consequential tool, small enough to finish while giving every Chapter 4-5 control real work to do.
